# First variations and an obstruction to one-vertex descent

This note supplies exact deformation formulas with a fixed lattice
projection. It then gives a minimal equal-mass strict mixed cap cover for
which moving any one exposed vertex in any nonzero continuous direction
increases the largest normalized cap mass to first order. A coordinated
movement of all vertices decreases every cap mass. Thus the result blocks
a proposed single-vertex descent principle; it does not block all possible
selective localization or classify global extremizers.

## 1. Polyhedral fiber-facet first variation

Consider a differentiable family of compact polytopes with fixed bounded
projection `P` in the integer coordinates. Suppose its positive fibers at
the finite set `J=P intersect Z^n` have representations

    K_z(t)={x:a_j(t) dot x<=b_j(t,z), j=1,...,N},

where the coefficient functions are differentiable at zero. Assume every
`K_z(0)` is full-dimensional and that constraints with zero continuous
normal remain valid and can be discarded. All other constraints have
nonzero continuous normal at zero. These explicit hypotheses permit an
ordinary boundary derivative; this is not a claim about families in which
positive-dimensional fibers are born from zero-dimensional ones.

Let `G` be a facet of `K_z(0)`, with outward continuous unit normal
`n_G`. Let `I_G` contain all inequality indices that are equalities on the
whole facet. For `j in I_G`, write `a_j(0)=kappa_j n_G`, where
`kappa_j>0`. Define the one-sided outward normal velocity

    v_G(x)=min_{j in I_G}
       [b_j'(0,z)-a_j'(0) dot x]/kappa_j, x in G.   (1)

Then, for the indicated positive parameter direction,

    d/dt|_{0+} vol_d(K_z(t))
       =sum_G int_G v_G(x) dH_{d-1}(x).            (2)

Repeated or coincident active inequalities are deliberately retained in
(1). Selecting just one such inequality could give the wrong derivative.
For a direction in the opposite parameter sense, reverse all coefficient
derivatives and apply (1)-(2) again; a single two-sided derivative need
not exist at a redundant-constraint transition.

Here is a direct justification. A strict interior point of `K_z(0)` has
positive slack in every nonzero-normal inequality and remains strictly
feasible for small parameter changes. Contraction towards this point
converts points feasible at time zero into feasible points at time `t`
with displacement `O(t)`; the reverse contraction does the same from
time `t` to zero. Uniform boundedness follows from boundedness at zero:
on the continuous unit sphere the maximum of the finitely many outward
normal scalar products has a positive minimum, which persists for small
coefficient changes. Consequently the Hausdorff distance is `O(t)`.
Away from the boundaries of its facets, an initial boundary point is
subject only to the inequalities in `I_G`. Substituting
`x+t s n_G` into these inequalities and dividing by `t` shows that the
largest allowable `s` tends to exactly (1), uniformly on compact patches
inside the facet. Fubini in the normal coordinate gives each patch's
volume derivative as its velocity integral. The symmetric difference of
the bodies lies in an `O(t)` boundary neighborhood. Patches near the
lower-dimensional facet boundaries contribute at most a constant times
`t` times their boundary-neighborhood area; divided by `t`, this tends
to zero as the patch cutoff shrinks. There are finitely many facets.
This proves (2). For `d=1`, facets are endpoints with counting measure,
and the argument is the familiar endpoint-length derivative.

For example, shifting a single nonredundant fiber inequality

    a dot x<=b(z)+t, a!=0,

gives outward normal speed `1/|a|` on its facet and zero speed on the
other facets, hence derivative `H_{d-1}(G_z)/|a|`. Such a shift can be
implemented globally by moving a polytope facet while keeping separate
vertical inequalities for its projection fixed, provided the affected
fibers stay full-dimensional as specified above.

## 2. Closed-cap derivatives, including coincident boundaries

Fix a closed ambient halfspace `H`, and restrict it to each fiber.
For a vertical halfspace, each restriction is the whole continuous space
or the empty set, independent of the parameter, so its contribution is
the full fiber derivative (2) or zero. The following formulas concern
nonvertical halfspaces.
On a facet patch where the cap boundary does not coincide with the whole
facet, the derivative of its captured volume is

    int_{G intersect int(H_z)} v_G dH_{d-1}.         (3)

A transverse boundary intersection has zero facet measure and contributes
nothing extra. If the cap boundary coincides with the facet, let the
outward coordinate from `K_z(0)` be `s`, with the original body locally
on `s<=0`:

* If the cap is `s<=0`, its derivative contribution is
  `int_G min(v_G,0) dH_{d-1}`.
* If the cap is `s>=0`, its derivative contribution is
  `int_G max(v_G,0) dH_{d-1}`.

Indeed a newly added strip on `s>0` belongs only to the latter cap, while
a removed strip on `s<0` belongs only to the former. These are one-sided
formulas and include the case in which the initial cap has zero volume.
They avoid silently discarding a whole facet merely because the ambient
cap is closed. Sum (3) and the appropriate coincident-facet terms over all
facets and integer fibers to obtain the unnormalized cap derivative `A_i`.
Write `A` for the derivative of total mixed volume `M` from (2). Then

    p_i'= (A_i-p_i A)/M, p_i=vol_MI(S intersect H_i)/M. (4)

For finitely many fixed caps and their maximum `F=max_i p_i`, the
one-sided directional derivative is

    F'=max_{i:p_i(0)=F(0)} p_i'.                   (5)

This follows by the finite expansions `p_i(t)=p_i(0)+t p_i'+o(t)`:
initially inactive indices stay separated from the maximum for small
`t`. In particular, with all cap masses equal, decreasing the maximum
requires every active quotient in (4) to be negative. A sign condition
on total volume alone cannot establish this.

## 3. A minimal strict cap cover with no one-vertex descent

Fix `n>=0,d>=1`, put `N=2^n`, and let `T` be a `d`-simplex with vertices
`t_0,...,t_d`, barycentric coordinates `lambda_0,...,lambda_d`, centroid
`g`, and volume `V`. Thus each `lambda_i` is affine, their sum is one,
and `lambda_i(g)=1/(d+1)`. Set

    C=[0,1]^n x T,
    S={0,1}^n x T,
    0<c<1/(d+1), q=(1-c)^d.

For every binary integer vertex `v`, define the affine function

    ell_v(z)=sum_{j:v_j=0} z_j +sum_{j:v_j=1}(1-z_j).

Its value is zero at `v` and a positive integer at every other binary
vertex. With the empty sum convention for `n=0`, define

    H_{v,i}={ (z,x):lambda_i(x)-2 ell_v(z)>=c },
    v in {0,1}^n, i=0,...,d.                       (6)

These are closed halfspaces with nonzero continuous normals. A cap in
(6) captures no other integer fiber: there `lambda_i<=1` and
`ell_v>=1`. Its conditional mass in its own fiber is `q`, by the usual
simplex cap homothety. Thus every normalized cap mass equals

    tau=q/N.                                      (7)

Their open interiors cover `S`: at any point of a simplex, some
`lambda_i>=1/(d+1)>c`. The cover is inclusion-minimal and has strict
exclusive interior witnesses. To see this, in each fiber choose a point
close enough to vertex `t_i` that `lambda_i>c` and all other barycentric
coordinates are positive and less than `c`. It is strictly inside cap
`(v,i)` and strictly outside every other cap. There are exactly
`N(d+1)=2^n(d+1)` caps.

Choose one exposed vertex `(v,t_j)` of the ambient product polytope and
move it to `(v,t_j+t h)`, for a nonzero vector `h in R^d`; all other
vertices stay fixed. Call the resulting convex hull `C_t`.
Its lattice projection is exactly unchanged. At every integer cube
vertex `w!=v`, its fiber remains `T`, since the extremality of `w` in
the cube prevents convex combinations using generators at other indices.
At `v`, the fiber is the simplex `T_t` with only vertex `t_j` moved.
For sufficiently small `|t|`, it is full-dimensional and all the strict
cover and witness conditions persist. The isolation of different fibers
by (6) also persists, since the gap in their integer term is at least two.

The affine map carrying `T` to `T_t` is

    X_t=X+t lambda_j(X)h.

Put `r_i=grad(lambda_i) dot h`, so `sum_i r_i=0`, and not all `r_i`
vanish. The determinant lemma gives

    V_t=V(1+t r_j), V_t'/V=r_j.                    (8)

Let `Q_i(t)` be the conditional probability of `lambda_i(X_t)>=c` for
uniform `X` in `T`; the affine image is uniform in `T_t`. The exact
derivatives are

    Q_i'(0)=D_{ij} r_i,
    D_{ij}=d c(1-c)^{d-1} if i=j,
    D_{ij}=(1-c)^d=q if i!=j.                      (9)

To verify (9), `lambda_i(X)` has density
`d(1-s)^{d-1}` on `(0,1)`. Conditional on `lambda_i(X)=c`, one has
`lambda_j=c` if `j=i`, while symmetry of the remaining barycentric
coordinates gives conditional mean `(1-c)/d` otherwise. The derivative
of the tail threshold under
`lambda_i(X_t)=lambda_i(X)+t lambda_j(X)r_i` is the density at `c`
times the conditional mean of `lambda_j` there, times `r_i`. This can
also be obtained directly by integrating over the `O(t)` slab around
the section `lambda_i=c`; its boundary is interior because `0<c<1`.
It yields precisely (9), with all `D_{ij}>0`.

The total mass is `(N-1)V+V_t`. The normalized derivatives of the caps
belonging to the affected fiber are consequently

    p_{v,i}'=(1/N)D_{ij}r_i
               +q(N-1)r_j/N^2.                   (10)

Every cap at an unaffected fiber has derivative

    p_{w,i}'=-q r_j/N^2, w!=v.                     (11)

If `N=1`, (10) has no second term and some `r_i>0`, so one derivative
is positive. If `N>=2` and `r_j<0`, every derivative in (11) is positive.
If `N>=2` and `r_j>=0`, choose an index with `r_i>0`; both terms in
(10) are then nonnegative and the first is strictly positive. Thus in
every case some cap derivative is strictly positive. By (5),

    d/dt|_{0+} max_{w,i} p_{w,i}(t)>0              (12)

for every nonzero continuous displacement of any single exposed vertex.
Applying this result to `-h` covers the opposite direction as well.
No ordinary one-vertex perturbation provides descent for this objective.

## 4. A coordinated deformation does give strict descent

The obstruction is specifically to local one-vertex moves. Simultaneously
replace every fiber by

    T(t)=g+(1+t)(T-g), t>0.

The lattice projection remains fixed, and the cap isolation and strict
cover remain valid for small `t`. The uniform conditional cap threshold
in original barycentric coordinates is

    c(t)=1/(d+1)+(c-1/(d+1))/(1+t).

All fibers have the same changing volume, so the normalized cap masses
are all `(1-c(t))^d/N`. Their derivatives at zero are

    -[d/N](1-c)^{d-1}(1/(d+1)-c)<0.               (13)

This contrast shows exactly what a deformation proof would need: a
coordinated change satisfying all active inequalities, rather than an
assumption that some exposed vertex can always be moved favorably.

For the entirely rational case `n=1,d=2,c=1/4`, there are six minimal
strict caps with common mass `9/32`. The coefficients in (9) are
`3/8` on the selected vertex index and `9/16` on the other indices.
The coordinated derivative in (13) is `-1/16`. These exact values and
the quotient-rule coefficients are checked by
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_selective_localization_first_variation.py`.

No minimizer existence claim is made. The set of strict cap covers is
open under small threshold changes. If every cap boundary cuts the
interior of a positive-volume fiber, slightly raising every threshold
strictly reduces every cap mass while retaining a sufficiently small
strict coverage margin. Consequently there is no minimum in that
particular open, freely thresholded class. Without this section-positivity
condition, cap-mass plateaus require separate treatment: nonvertical
normals alone do not ensure strict decrease. Any extremal argument must
specify its normalization and what happens when coverage or section
positivity is lost at a limit.
